title: True words aren't pretty
hook: true words aren't beautiful; the more the sage gives, the more he has (Tao Te Ching 81)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the small village: people who hear the neighbors' dogs and find their own food sweet. Your line was content at home. What did you notice on your own street? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

Two notes after a job interview. The first is from a recruiter: wonderful energy, so impressive, we'll be in touch. The second is from an old friend you asked to look at your answers: the second one rambled, and you never said why you want the job. One of those notes is lovely to read. The other is the one you'll actually use. Chapter eighty-one of the Tao Te Ching opens with that difference, and then, almost in the same breath, it turns to giving.
screen: `A LOVELY NOTE.` → `A USEFUL NOTE.` → `WHICH ONE IS TRUE?`

segments.voice: First, the opening pair. Words that are true aren't pretty, the chapter says, and pretty words aren't true. It's a mirror line: turn it around and it still holds. That doesn't mean every kind word is a lie. It means polish is not the same thing as truth, and sometimes the polish is there to cover something. Second, two more pairs in the same shape. The good don't argue, and those who argue aren't good. Those who really know aren't widely learned, and the widely learned don't really know. These sound harsh until you remember the whole book. Back in chapter seventy-one, the best knowing was knowing you don't know. Here, piling up facts and winning debates are both set to one side. Third, the turn, and it's the line our carry comes from. The sage doesn't hoard. The more the sage does for others, the more the sage has. The more the sage gives to others, the more the sage's own store grows. Read that as plain arithmetic and it's nonsense. Read it as a life, and it starts to make sense: a teacher who explains a thing understands it better; a cook who feeds people gets a full table. Fourth, the chapter's closing lines. Heaven's way, the chapter says, is to benefit and not harm. The sage's way is to act and not contend. After all the water, valleys, and uncarved wood, the chapter settles on giving without fighting. Outside the book, it's the plain sentence instead of the shiny one, and the thing handed over without a receipt.
screen: `TRUE WORDS AREN'T PRETTY.` · `THE ARGUER, THE PILED-UP LEARNING.` · `THE MORE HE GIVES, THE MORE HE HAS.` · `BENEFIT, DON'T HARM. ACT, DON'T FIGHT.` · then, large: `THE MORE I GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something away. Settle and let the breath do its own work for a few rounds. Then look around your life for one thing you've been holding on to that someone else could use. A coat in the closet. A book you've finished. An hour. A skill, like fixing a bike or reading a lease. Or a true word someone needs, said plainly and kindly. Pick one. Picture handing it over, and notice what's left in your own hands afterward. The bell holds the time.
True words aren't pretty. Chapter eighty-one: true words aren't beautiful, and beautiful words aren't true; the more the sage gives, the more the sage has. Today's word.
Your line: the more I give. Today, give away one thing, an object, an hour, or a plain true word, and don't keep count of it. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty-one as a summary of the sage's way: speak plainly, don't argue for the sake of winning, don't hoard, and find that giving to others leaves you with more.

match.prompt: the last chapter's pairs: tap them.

fork.setup: you're the sage. you have plenty, and people keep asking. what does chapter eighty-one say happens?
options: you store it up, so there's enough for later.
the more you give, the more you have.
you give until there's nothing left.
fork.reveal: the sage doesn't hoard. the more the sage does for others, the more the sage has; the more the sage gives, the more the sage's store grows.

original.note: Chinese: true words aren't beautiful, the opening of chapter eighty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: true words aren't pretty means honest people are blunt.
what it means: polish isn't truth; and giving, not hoarding, is how the sage's store grows.
what a scholar hears: the chapter is built from mirrored pairs, a shape the book uses elsewhere too, and it ends on 'act and don't contend', echoing earlier chapters on not fighting.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 81 (true words aren't beautiful, beautiful words aren't true; the good don't argue; those who know aren't widely learned; the sage doesn't hoard, and the more he gives the more he has; heaven benefits and doesn't harm, the sage acts and doesn't contend)
Tao Te Ching 71 (to know that you don't know is best; recalled)

notes: Chapter 81 is paraphrased; Legge's wording ('Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere') was not quoted because the writer could not confirm the whole passage word for word.

The teach calls this the final chapter and says the book closes on 'act and don't contend'; true of the received 81-chapter order. Some manuscripts order the chapters differently; confirm the path's framing.
Original 信言不美 (xìn yán bù měi) rendered 'SHIN yen boo MAY'; confirm.
'After eighty chapters of water, valleys, and uncarved wood' refers back to the path's own earlier days (like water, be the valley, plain silk, uncarved wood).

Editor: replaced 'the final chapter' / 'the last words of the book' with the chapter number (a fact about the text rather than the text); cut the count 'after eighty chapters'; softened 'readers often' and 'a shape the whole book uses'; varied the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
